claim: In vivo two-photon calcium imaging currently allows observation of the activity of multiple neurons up to ~900 µm below the cortical surface without cortical invasion.
source: In vivo two-photon calcium imaging currently allows us to observe the activity of multiple neurons up to ~900 µm below the cortical surface without cortical invasion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature in the field, as indicated by the context of the introduction discussing current capabilities.

claim: Using an 1100 nm laser that underfilled the back aperture of the objective together with red genetically encoded calcium indicators enables two-photon calcium imaging of the intact mouse brain and detection of neural activity up to 1200 μm from the cortical surface.
source: Here, we used an 1100 nm laser that underfilled the back aperture of the objective together with red genetically encoded calcium indicators to establish two-photon calcium imaging of the intact mouse brain and detect neural activity up to 1200 μm from the cortical surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including figures showing imaging at these depths.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging was obtained from the medial prefrontal cortex (the prelimbic area) and the hippocampal CA1 region.
source: This imaging was obtained from the medial prefrontal cortex (the prelimbic area) and the hippocampal CA1 region.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neural activity before water delivery repeated at a constant interval was higher in the prelimbic area than in layer 2/3 of the secondary motor area.
source: We found that neural activity before water delivery repeated at a constant interval was higher in the prelimbic area than in layer 2/3 of the secondary motor area.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data analysis presented in the results section.

claim: By exciting red-fluorescent calcium indicators with a laser at wavelengths of 1000–1100 nm through a cranial window, it is possible to image neural activity in the mouse sensory cortex at depths of 800–900 µm from the cortical surface (corresponding to layers 5 and 6).
source: Recent work demonstrates that by exciting red-fluorescent calcium indicators with a laser at wavelengths of 1000–1100 nm through a cranial window, it is possible to image neural activity in the mouse sensory cortex at depths of 800–900 µm from the cortical surface (corresponding to layers 5 and 6) (Dana et al., 2016; Tischbirek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: For functional imaging of deeper regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and basal ganglia, invasive penetration is unavoidable; it is necessary to insert a microlens or a microprism into the cortical tissue, or to remove the cortical tissue above the target region.
source: However, for functional imaging of deeper regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and basal ganglia, invasive penetration is unavoidable; it is necessary to insert a microlens or a microprism into the cortical tissue, or to remove the cortical tissue above the target region (Attardo et al., 2015; Dombeck et al., 2010; Low et al., 2014; Pilz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work describing current methods.

claim: The difficulty of deep imaging is mainly caused by refractive index mismatch and light scattering within the tissue.
source: The difficulty of deep imaging is mainly caused by refractive index mismatch and light scattering within the tissue (Helmchen and Denk, 2005; Tung et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Refractive index mismatch and light scattering can be weakened when objectives with low numerical aperture (NA) are used because the angle of light emitted from the objective is smaller and the light-path length within the tissue is shorter than when high NA objectives are used.
source: These can be weakened when objectives with low numerical aperture (NA) are used because the angle of light emitted from the objective is smaller and the light-path length within the tissue is shorter than when high NA objectives are used.
evidence: This is based on established optical principles and theoretical understanding.

claim: When low NA objectives are used, the spatial resolution and collection efficiency of emitted fluorescent signals are worse than when high NA objectives are used.
source: However, when low NA objectives are used, the spatial resolution and collection efficiency of emitted fluorescent signals are worse than when high NA objectives are used.
evidence: This is based on established optical principles.

claim: If a high NA objective is used in conjunction with underfilling of the back aperture by the excitation laser, the collection efficiency of the fluorescent signal remains high.
source: If a high NA objective is used in conjunction with underfilling of the back aperture by the excitation laser, the collection efficiency of the fluorescent signal remains high.
evidence: This is based on optical theory and is a key principle underlying the method.

claim: If the effective NA for the excitation light is small but sufficient to resolve single neurons (10–15 μm along the Z axis), this technique may increase the maximal depth for two-photon calcium imaging of neuronal somata.
source: If the effective NA for the excitation light is small but sufficient to resolve single neurons (10–15 μm along the Z axis; Lecoq et al., 2014), this technique may increase the maximal depth for two-photon calcium imaging of neuronal somata.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical considerations and cited prior work.

claim: The underfilling technique has been theoretically predicted and partially demonstrated in the skin.
source: Although this technique has been theoretically predicted and partially demonstrated in the skin (Helmchen and Denk, 2005; Tung et al., 2004), it has not been applied to deep imaging of neural activity in behaving animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The underfilling technique has not been applied to deep imaging of neural activity in behaving animals.
source: Although this technique has been theoretically predicted and partially demonstrated in the skin (Helmchen and Denk, 2005; Tung et al., 2004), it has not been applied to deep imaging of neural activity in behaving animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Long-wavelength excitation light and red-fluorescent genetically encoded calcium indicators are suitable for deep imaging because light scattering is weaker at longer wavelengths.
source: In addition, long-wavelength excitation light and red-fluorescent genetically encoded calcium indicators (red GECIs; Dana et al., 2016; Inoue et al., 2015; Ohkura et al., 2012) are suitable for deep imaging because light scattering is weaker at longer wavelengths.
evidence: This is based on established optical principles and cited prior work on red GECIs.

claim: By underfilling high NA objectives to reduce the effective NA for excitation to approximately 0.5 and exciting red GECIs with an 1100-nm laser, the activity of multiple neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex (the prelimbic [PL] area) and the hippocampal CA1 region at depths of 1.0–1.2 mm in behaving mice can be detected without the need for invasive penetration or removal of cortical tissue.
source: Here, we demonstrate that by underfilling high NA objectives to reduce the effective NA for excitation to approximately 0.5 and exciting red GECIs with an 1100-nm laser, we could detect the activity of multiple neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex (the prelimbic [PL] area) and the hippocampal CA1 region at depths of 1.0–1.2 mm in behaving mice without the need for invasive penetration or removal of cortical tissue.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The back aperture of a high NA (1.00) objective was underfilled with a diameter-narrowed 1100 nm laser beam (1/e2-width was 7.2 mm, compared with the back aperture of 14.4 mm).
source: To reduce the effective NA, the back aperture of a high NA (1.00) objective was underfilled with a diameter-narrowed 1100 nm laser beam (1/e2-width was 7.2 mm, compared with the back aperture of 14.4 mm) (Figure 1A; Matsuzaki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the experimental setup and Figure 1A.

claim: The effective NA was calculated to be roughly 0.5.
source: The effective NA was calculated to be roughly 0.5 (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the experimental setup.

claim: When the objective was underfilled, the full-widths at half-maximum (FWHMs) were 2.28 ± 0.05 μm (mean ± s.d., n = 5 beads) laterally and 6.95 ± 0.13 μm (n = 5 beads) axially.
source: When the objective was underfilled, the full-widths at half-maximum (FWHMs) were 2.28 ± 0.05 μm (mean ± s.d., n = 5 beads) laterally and 6.95 ± 0.13 μm (n = 5 beads) axially (Figure 1Bi).
evidence: This is experimental data measuring spatial resolution with fluorescent beads.

claim: When the objective was overfilled, the FWHMs were 2.15 ± 0.05 μm (n = 4 beads) laterally and 4.37 ± 0.06 μm (n = 4 beads) axially.
source: These values were greater than the FWHMs of 2.15 ± 0.05 μm (n = 4 beads) laterally and 4.37 ± 0.06 μm (n = 4 beads) axially when the objective was overfilled (Figure 1Bii)
evidence: This is experimental data measuring spatial resolution with fluorescent beads.

claim: The FWHM values obtained with underfilling are comparable with those used for two-photon calcium imaging of multiple neurons with cellular resolution.
source: but comparable with those used for two-photon calcium imaging of multiple neurons with cellular resolution (Lecoq et al., 2014; Sadakane et al., 2015; Stirman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim compares the measured values to those reported in cited literature.

claim: For all depths, the mean bright fluorescent signal was higher in the underfilled than in the overfilled configuration.
source: For all depths, the mean bright fluorescent signal (Kobat et al., 2009), which was assumed to reflect the fluorescence from tdTomato-expressing neurons, was higher in the underfilled than in the overfilled configuration (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data comparing fluorescence signals between configurations.

claim: The number of circles detected by the Hough transform method was similar between the two configurations at depths of 200–600 µm from the cortical surface.
source: The number of circles detected by the Hough transform method (see Materials and methods), which is assumed to reflect the number of fluorescent neuronal somata, was similar between the two configurations at depths of 200–600 µm from the cortical surface (Figure 1F,G and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data analyzing neuronal detection at different depths.

claim: The number of circles detected at depths > 600 µm was larger in the underfilled than in the overfilled configuration.
source: However, the number of circles detected at depths > 600 µm was larger in the underfilled than in the overfilled configuration (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is experimental data showing improved detection at greater depths with underfilling.

claim: Underfilling the objective was more effective at detecting neuronal morphology at depths > 600 µm.
source: Thus, underfilling the objective was more effective at detecting neuronal morphology at depths > 600 µm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing underfilled and overfilled configurations.

claim: Using laser power of 170–180 mW at the front aperture of the objective, calcium transients were detected at depths of 1.0–1.2 mm.
source: Using laser power of 170–180 mW at the front aperture of the objective, we detected calcium transients at depths of 1.0–1.2 mm (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is experimental data showing successful detection of neural activity at deep locations.

claim: The laser power used (170-180 mW) was higher than that used for two-photon imaging of cortical layers 5 and/or 6 in previous studies.
source: This laser power was higher than that used for two-photon imaging of cortical layers 5 and/or 6 (the maximum power used was: 150 mW in Dana et al., 2016; 114 mW in Masamizu et al., 2014; 170 mW in Tischbirek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to laser powers reported in cited literature.

claim: The immunoreactivity after 15- or 30-min imaging at 800–1100 µm depths was not different from that in negative control mice.
source: The immunoreactivity after 15- or 30-min imaging at 800–1100 µm depths was not different from that in negative control mice (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunostaining assays showing no tissue damage.

claim: Imaging at 300–400 µm depths with an 1100 nm laser caused significantly higher anti-GFAP and anti-Iba1 immunoreactivity than deep imaging.
source: By contrast, imaging at 300–400 µm depths with an 1100 nm laser caused significantly higher anti-GFAP and anti-Iba1 immunoreactivity than deep imaging (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunostaining assays showing tissue damage at shallow depths.

claim: Imaging at 200–300 µm depths with a 920 nm laser in the slow scanning mode caused significantly higher immunoreactivity of all antibodies than deep imaging.
source: Imaging at 200–300 µm depths with a 920 nm laser in the slow scanning mode caused significantly higher immunoreactivity of all antibodies than deep imaging (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from immunostaining assays showing tissue damage with different imaging parameters.

claim: 15–30 min two-photon imaging of the deep area with an 1100 nm laser at 180 mW power did not cause any apparent histological injury.
source: However, 15–30 min two-photon imaging of the deep area with an 1100 nm laser at 180 mW power did not cause any apparent histological injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunostaining data.

claim: There was no difference in the mean inferred activities between the first 5-min period and the last 5-min period of a 25-min continuous imaging session at 900–1100 µm depths in awake mice.
source: In a 25-min continuous imaging session at 900–1100 µm depths in awake mice, we compared the activity of imaged neurons in the first 5-min period with that in the last 5-min period. There was no difference in the mean inferred activities (by a constrained non-negative matrix factorization algorithm; Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016) between the two periods (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data showing that neural activity was not affected by imaging.

claim: Two-photon imaging of the deep area with ~180 mW laser power did not appear to alter neural excitability.
source: This indicates that two-photon imaging of the deep area with ~180 mW laser power did not appear to alter neural excitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural activity data.

claim: As each conditioning session progressed, the licking response rate to water delivery increased and licking became faster.
source: As each session progressed (one session per day), the licking response rate to water delivery increased and licking became faster (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is behavioral data showing learning during conditioning.

claim: The imaging fields were classified into three areas according to depth: the superficial area (100–300 µm, corresponding to layer 2/3 in the secondary motor area, M2), the middle area (300–800 µm, corresponding to layer 5 in M2), and the deep area (800–1200 µm, roughly corresponding to layer 6 in M2 and the PL area).
source: The imaging fields were classified into three areas according to depth (Paxinos and Franklin, 2007): the superficial area (100–300 µm, corresponding to layer 2/3 in the secondary motor area, M2), the middle area (300–800 µm, corresponding to layer 5 in M2), and the deep area (800–1200 µm, roughly corresponding to layer 6 in M2 and the PL area).
evidence: This is a methodological classification based on anatomical reference and depth measurements.

claim: In all three areas, approximately 50% of neurons showed a peak in the mean (trial-averaged) activity during the 5 s after water delivery.
source: In all three areas, approximately 50% of neurons showed a peak in the mean (trial-averaged) activity during the 5 s after water delivery (Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which was presumably related to licking and water acquisition (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data analyzing neural activity patterns.

claim: Approximately 30% of neurons in all three areas showed a peak in the mean activity during the 10 s before water delivery (pre-reward period).
source: Additionally, approximately 30% of neurons in all three areas showed a peak in the mean activity during the 10 s before water delivery (pre-reward period; Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data analyzing neural activity patterns.

claim: The sequential distribution of the times of peak activity was not an artifact of ordering the neurons according to the time of peak activity, as the ratio of the mean activity around the peak activity to the baseline activity (ridge-to-background ratio) was significantly higher than that of shuffled data.
source: The sequential distribution of the times of peak activity was not an artifact of ordering the neurons according to the time of peak activity, as the ratio of the mean activity around the peak activity to the baseline activity (ridge-to-background ratio; Harvey et al., 2012) was significantly higher than that of shuffled data (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis validating the observed neural activity patterns.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the times of peak activity of two randomly separated groups of trials was higher in the deep area than in the superficial area.
source: To determine whether the activity pattern across trials was stable for individual neurons with peak activity during the pre-reward period, we calculated the correlation coefficient between the times of peak activity of two randomly separated groups of trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A,B; see details in Materials and methods section) and found that it was higher in the deep area than in the superficial area (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is experimental data showing trial-to-trial stability of neural activity.

claim: The PL neurons reliably code the neural activity during the pre-reward period.
source: This indicates that the PL neurons reliably code the neural activity during the pre-reward period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trial-to-trial stability analysis.

claim: CA1 GFP-expressing neurons can be detected by two-photon microscopy in 4-week-old mice, but not in 6- to 9-week-old mice.
source: CA1 GFP-expressing neurons can be detected by two-photon microscopy in 4-week-old mice, but not in 6- to 9-week-old mice (Kawakami et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: When the focal plane was deepened below the white matter to depths of 900–1000 µm, densely distributed fluorescent neurons typically located in the CA1 pyramidal layer were observed.
source: When we deepened the focal plane below the white matter to depths of 900–1000 µm, we observed densely distributed fluorescent neurons typically located in the CA1 pyramidal layer (Figure 5B,C and Video 4), as described previously (Dombeck et al., 2010), and clearly detected spontaneous calcium transients from these neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is experimental data showing successful imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: No cell death or strong damage was apparent after 15 min of imaging in the hippocampus.
source: No cell death or strong damage was apparent after 15 min of imaging (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is experimental data from histological examination.

claim: Neural morphology or activity could not be detected in the CA1 region of mice when they were 3 months old.
source: By contrast, we could not detect any neural morphology or activity in the CA1 region of the mice when they were 3 months old.
evidence: This is an experimental observation about age-dependent imaging limitations.

claim: The majority of active neurons in hippocampal CA1 showed peak activity 0–5 s after water delivery.
source: The majority of active neurons showed peak activity 0–5 s after water delivery (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is experimental data analyzing neural activity patterns in the hippocampus.

claim: The time of peak activity of neurons showing peak activity during the pre-reward period was not stable across trials in the hippocampus.
source: The time of peak activity of neurons showing peak activity during the pre-reward period was not stable across trials (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is experimental data showing lack of trial-to-trial stability in hippocampal neurons.

claim: Underfilling the objective was effective for deep (600–1200 µm from the cortical surface) imaging of neural morphology and activity in the mouse brain over the course of several days.
source: Here, we demonstrated that underfilling the objective was effective for deep (600–1200 µm from the cortical surface) imaging of neural morphology and activity in the mouse brain over the course of several days.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: The effectiveness of underfilling may be due not only to reduced light scattering but also to the high fluorescent signal in the underfilled configuration; fluorescence is integrated over a larger focal volume in the underfilled configuration than in the overfilled configuration.
source: This may be due not only to reduced light scattering but also to the high fluorescent signal in the underfilled configuration; fluorescence is integrated over a larger focal volume in the underfilled configuration than in the overfilled configuration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed results.

claim: 15- and 30-min imaging did not produce any apparent morphological or functional damage to the brain tissue.
source: However, we confirmed that 15- and 30-min imaging did not produce any apparent morphological or functional damage to the brain tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunostaining and neural activity data.

claim: The lack of damage might be because the excitation (or density of photons) at the focal center is lower in the underfilled configuration than in the overfilled configuration and the heat derived from the 1100 nm photon absorbance is relatively low.
source: This might be because the excitation (or density of photons) at the focal center is lower in the underfilled configuration than in the overfilled configuration (Helmchen and Denk, 2005) and the heat derived from the 1100 nm photon absorbance is relatively low (Hale and Querry, 1973).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on cited optical principles.

claim: The infralimbic area at >1200 µm depths or the hippocampus in adult mice could not be imaged.
source: We could not image the infralimbic area at >1200 µm depths or the hippocampus in adult mice.
evidence: This is a limitation of the method as observed in the experiments.

claim: Adult hippocampus is difficult to image because, as the mouse becomes older, the myelination of the white matter increases.
source: Adult hippocampus is difficult to image because, as the mouse becomes older, the myelination of the white matter increases (Bockhorst et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an explanation based on cited literature about developmental changes.

claim: Three-photon calcium imaging with a 1300 nm laser with a high power per pulse (~60 nJ) can access adult hippocampal CA1 neurons.
source: A recent study demonstrated that three-photon calcium imaging with a 1300 nm laser with a high power per pulse (~60 nJ) can access adult hippocampal CA1 neurons (Ouzounov et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent published study.

claim: Light at around 1100 nm may also penetrate the highly myelinated white matter if a laser with higher average power or higher power per pulse is used.
source: This suggests that light at around 1100 nm may also penetrate the highly myelinated white matter if a laser with higher average power or higher power per pulse (Kawakami et al., 2015) is used (the power per pulse in this study was 2.3 nJ).
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison to other work and the current study's parameters.

claim: Reduction of the effective NA to ~0.35, introduction of adaptive optics to compensate for light scattering, and further improvement of the signal-to-noise ratio of red GECIs will be helpful for imaging multicellular activity in the infralimbic area and the hippocampus in adult intact mice.
source: In addition, reduction of the effective NA to ~0.35 (corresponding to an axial resolution of ~10 µm; Lecoq et al., 2014; Stirman et al., 2016), introduction of adaptive optics to compensate for light scattering (Ji et al., 2010), and further improvement of the signal-to-noise ratio of red GECIs (Dana et al., 2016; Inoue et al., 2015) will certainly be helpful for imaging multicellular activity in the infralimbic area and the hippocampus in adult intact mice.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements based on cited literature.

claim: The major disadvantage of reducing the effective NA is a decrease in spatial resolution.
source: The major disadvantage of reducing the effective NA is a decrease in spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about a trade-off in the method based on optical principles.

claim: The axial resolution of approximately 7 µm is sufficient to resolve single neurons and is unlikely to cause cross-talk between neurons closely located along the Z axis.
source: In this study, the axial resolution was approximately 7 µm, which is sufficient to resolve single neurons and is unlikely to cause cross-talk between neurons closely located along the Z axis (Lecoq et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an assessment of the method's resolution based on the measured value and cited literature.

claim: If dendritic branches and spines, and axonal branches and boutons, are the imaging target, then the spatial resolution may not be sufficient.
source: However, if dendritic branches and spines, and axonal branches and boutons, are the imaging target, then the spatial resolution may not be sufficient.
evidence: This is a speculation about limitations for subcellular imaging.

claim: When adaptive optics are used, YFP-expressing dendritic spines can be resolved at a depth of 600 µm.
source: When adaptive optics are used, YFP-expressing dendritic spines can be resolved at a depth of 600 µm (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: For deep imaging of subcellular activity, a slightly underfilled objective (with an effective NA of ~0.7) combined with adaptive optics may be useful.
source: Thus, for deep imaging of subcellular activity, a slightly underfilled objective (with an effective NA of ~0.7) combined with adaptive optics may be useful.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future approaches.

claim: Neural activity during the pre-reward period was more robust in the deep area (the PL area) than in the superficial area of the mFrC (M2).
source: We found that neural activity during the pre-reward period was more robust in the deep area (the PL area) than in the superficial area of the mFrC (M2).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings comparing neural activity across brain areas.

claim: The PL area is strongly related to the processing of motivation-, attention-, and reward-related information.
source: The PL area is strongly related to the processing of motivation-, attention-, and reward-related information (Friedman et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016b; Otis et al., 2017; Pinto and Dan, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: M2 is strongly related to action selection and motor planning.
source: whereas M2 is strongly related to action selection and motor planning (Li et al., 2015; Sul et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: PL activity during the pre-reward period might reflect the expectation of reward delivery, including motivation, reward prediction, or attention to the timing of the water delivery.
source: Thus, PL activity during the pre-reward period might reflect the expectation of reward delivery, including motivation, reward prediction, or attention to the timing of the water delivery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed neural activity.

claim: The conditioning in this study did not require any change in mouse brain state before water delivery.
source: However, the conditioning in this study did not require any change in mouse brain state before water delivery.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the intact brain, it is easy to change the field of view parallel to the cortical surface.
source: In the intact brain, it is easy to change the field of view parallel to the cortical surface.
evidence: This is a statement about an advantage of the non-invasive approach.

claim: An 8-mm-wide glass window can be used for long-term imaging of the whole dorsal neocortex in the mouse.
source: An 8-mm-wide glass window can be used for long-term imaging of the whole dorsal neocortex in the mouse (Kim et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Objectives with wide fields of view (>3 mm) developed for two-photon imaging can cover the mFrC and the neocortex lying above the hippocampus.
source: Objectives with wide fields of view (>3 mm) developed for two-photon imaging (Sofroniew et al., 2016; Stirman et al., 2016; Tsai et al., 2015) can cover the mFrC and the neocortex lying above the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is based on cited literature about available imaging technology.

claim: The hippocampus connects the mFrC through the thalamus and the entorhinal cortex.
source: The hippocampus connects the mFrC through the thalamus and the entorhinal cortex (Jin and Maren, 2015; Varela et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work on brain connectivity.

claim: The hippocampus is thought to associate spatial, temporal, and reward information, which are required for goal-directed decision-making.
source: and is thought to associate spatial, temporal, and reward information, which are required for goal-directed decision-making (Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The pre-reward activity in hippocampal CA1 neurons was not stable, likely because the conditioning period in the young mice was not sufficient to form such activity.
source: Here, the pre-reward activity in hippocampal CA1 neurons was not stable, likely because the conditioning period in the young mice was not sufficient to form such activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Deep and wide-field two-photon calcium imaging of the intact brain will substantially aid our understanding of the brain circuits that integrate multimodal information in decision-making.
source: Deep and wide-field two-photon calcium imaging of the intact brain will substantially aid our understanding of the brain circuits that integrate multimodal information in decision-making.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future impact of the method.
